children: By Renae Dyer

Sterling rose to a six-week high against the euro Wednesday following upwardly revised U.K. economic growth data and after U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham promised fiscal discipline and improved ties with the EU.
The Office for National Statistics said Wednesday that the U.K. economy grew 0.5% in the second quarter, an unexpected revision from the previous estimate of 0.4%.
"It continues the strong start to the year for the U.K. economy which expanded by 0.6% in the first quarter," MUFG Bank senior currency analyst Lee Hardman said in a note.
Stronger growth will encourage the Bank of England to raise interest rates soon if higher energy prices prove more persistent, adding support to the pound, he said.

Sterling rose to a six-week high of 0.8538 per euro in midday European trade, LSEG data showed. Against the dollar, the U.K. currency rose 0.5% to a one-week high of $1.3311, also supported by below-forecast U.S. PCE inflation data damping U.S. rate-rise expectations.
Following the U.K. data, money markets priced an 81% chance of the BOE raising rates by 25 basis points at its next meeting in November, according to LSEG.

Burnham told the ruling Labour Party's annual conference on Tuesday that he plans to stick to the fiscal rules, easing concerns about risks to already-stretched public finances, while he would spell out the options for the U.K.'s relations with the EU at a U.K.-EU summit later this year.

He later signaled that re-joining the EU was among the options he would discuss at the summit. He told the BBC that the options included entering a customs union, rejoining the single market or "go all the way."
"It opens up the possibility for a potential reverse-Brexit trade for the pound in the future," MUFG Bank's Hardman said.
Sterling has never fully recovered from the 2016 Brexit referendum, remaining well below levels against the euro seen before the vote.

"While the prospect of a closer relationship with the EU under Burnham may eventually be a sterling positive factor, there are many obstacles before the pound will start to reflect this issue," Rabobank senior foreign exchange strategist Jane Foley said in a note.

"Not only will the U.K. electorate have to be brought on side (though recent U.K. opinion polls are reflecting a clear preference in favour of EU membership), but it is unclear how the EU would respond."

Burnham's speech at the Labour conference also outlined changes to pensions and plans to strengthen control of water companies, build a national care service and create a public body to invest in the electricity grid.

The U.K. government's signals that it is committed to sticking to fiscal rules helped lower yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts. Yields on 10-year gilts fell 1.8 basis points to 5.379%, according to Tradeweb.

While the gilt market took Burnham's fiscal plans in its stride, investors will want to see the arithmetic in the October 28 autumn budget, Monex Europe analysts said in a note. Sterling is also at risk of falling as the budget draws nearer, they said.
"If the current Labour party leadership team maintains its promise to respect the fiscal rules, there may be room for a post-budget relief rally in the pound, Rabobank's Foley said.
However, given Burnham's spending plans, this suggests more tax rises, which have negative growth connotations, she said.

Sterling investors could be cautious ahead of the budget but headwinds to eurozone growth and political uncertainties in France and Germany could limit the euro's potential to rise against sterling into the new year, she said. Rabobank anticipates sterling will hold its recent range against the euro in coming weeks.
